planting.note: Direct sow in spring in very well-drained, dry, gravelly or sandy, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; plains zinnia is native to shortgrass prairie and high plains grassland and needs sharp drainage far more than it needs fertility.

directions: Direct sow into lean, sharply drained, gravelly or sandy soil in full sun; plains zinnia is a low, spreading perennial relative of the common bedding zinnia, native from the high plains south through the Chihuahuan Desert. Narrow gray-green leaves and small, bright golden-yellow flowers with a darker center cover the low mounding to creeping mats from late spring through fall, drawing butterflies and native bees even in extreme summer heat and drought. It spreads slowly by underground rhizomes to form a dense, tough, walkable groundcover in xeriscape beds, dry slopes, and rock gardens, and is essentially untroubled by pests, disease, or deer once established. Avoid rich soil, extra irrigation, and winter-wet sites, all of which shorten its life and encourage rot in this drought-adapted, deep-rooted species.

planting.note: Plant rooted offsets (pups) in spring in gritty, mineral, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; claret cup is among the most cold-hardy of all North American cacti, tolerating winter lows well below 0°F where soil stays dry.

directions: Plant rooted offsets in a raised bed, berm, or crevice garden of coarse gravel, decomposed granite, or mineral scree in full sun, keeping soil dry through winter to prevent rot; unlike most cacti, claret cup survives severe cold as long as its roots stay dry and unfrozen-wet. Clumps of cylindrical, spine-covered stems slowly multiply into mounds of 20 or more heads, topped in mid- to late spring by brilliant scarlet-red, cup-shaped flowers that are among the showiest of any hardy cactus and are a favored early-season hummingbird nectar source. Water sparingly only during active spring and summer growth and withhold water entirely from late fall through winter. Established clumps are essentially indestructible in the right drainage and are outstanding for rock gardens, dry berms, and desert-style xeriscape plantings from the high plains through the Southwest.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall so winter cold moist-stratifies the seed naturally, into well-drained, dry to average, limestone-based or clay-loam soil in full sun; Engelmann's daisy is a deep-taprooted Great Plains prairie native adapted to heavy soils and periodic drought.

directions: Direct sow in fall into well-drained clay-loam or limestone soil in full sun, allowing winter cold to break seed dormancy naturally; a deep, thick taproot makes established plants extremely drought tolerant but hard to transplant, so site it where it can stay long term. Coarse, deeply lobed, rough-textured basal leaves send up branching flower stalks topped with cheerful yellow daisy-like blooms from spring through early summer, and again after fall rains, that are heavily visited by native bees and small butterflies. Foliage dies back somewhat in peak summer heat and regrows with cooler fall weather, so avoid judging plants on midsummer appearance alone. A true low-input, tough tallgrass and shortgrass prairie perennial, it is an excellent choice for naturalistic prairie restorations, pollinator meadows, and dry, unirrigated beds across the southern Great Plains.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost with a 3–4 week cold-moist stratification for best germination, or set out nursery divisions in spring, into very well-drained, dry, gravelly, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun.

directions: Plant in gritty, sharply drained, lean soil in full sun; pineleaf penstemon is a compact, woody-based, evergreen subshrub from the mountains of the American Southwest and northern Mexico, with narrow, needle-like leaves that persist year-round and give the plant its pine-like texture even when not in bloom. Slender, tubular, brilliant orange-red to scarlet flowers cover the mounding plants from late spring through summer and are outstanding hummingbird forage, reblooming readily if lightly sheared after the first flush. It is among the most heat- and drought-tolerant of all penstemons, thriving in rock gardens, dry borders, and gravel mulch plantings where excess moisture and rich soil would quickly rot it. Shear back lightly in early spring to remove winter-damaged growth and keep the mound dense and compact.

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring, even before the last frost date, into well-drained, dry, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; Tahoka daisy self-seeds freely and is often easiest to establish by fall sowing where winters are mild.

directions: Direct sow into lean, well-drained, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun as soon as soil can be worked, since seedlings tolerate light frost; Tahoka daisy is a fast, drought-tough Great Plains and Southwest native annual with finely cut, ferny, aromatic foliage. Large lavender-blue, yellow-centered daisy flowers open in profusion from late spring through fall, closing at night and on cloudy days, and are a strong draw for native bees and butterflies. Plants sprawl and self-seed generously in loose, dry soil, so it naturalizes readily in wildflower meadows and gravel gardens once introduced, often returning from seed for years with no replanting. It needs no supplemental fertilizer and little to no irrigation once seedlings are established, making it a reliable, low-maintenance filler for hot, dry, sunny sites.

planting.note: Set rooted cuttings or container-grown plants in spring into very well-drained, dry, rocky or sandy, alkaline soil in full sun; trailing indigo bush is propagated almost exclusively from stem cuttings to preserve its low, even groundcover habit.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings in sharply drained, rocky or sandy, alkaline soil in full sun, spacing wide since a single plant spreads into a dense mat 5 to 8 feet across within a couple of seasons. Small, silvery-gray, pinnately compound leaves cover trailing, woody stems that root as they spread, and clusters of small purple, pea-like flowers appear in spring, drawing bees and providing light seasonal color over the silver foliage. Extremely drought tolerant once established, it needs no supplemental irrigation in the low desert and is commonly used as a large-scale erosion-control groundcover on slopes, banks, and parking lot islands throughout its native Chihuahuan Desert range. Prune back hard every few years to rejuvenate woody, overgrown mats and keep the silvery foliage dense and fresh.
sources: Arizona Municipal Water Users Association (Xeriscape Plant Guide)

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into thin, rocky, limestone-derived soil in partial shade to full sun; Roemer's phlox is a Texas Hill Country endemic annual that germinates with fall rains, overwinters as a small rosette, and blooms the following spring.

directions: Direct sow in fall onto thin, rocky, limestone-influenced soil in dappled shade to full sun beneath oaks and junipers, mimicking the woodland-edge slopes and canyons where this Texas Hill Country endemic grows wild. Seedlings overwinter as small rosettes and bolt in early spring into loose sprays of five-petaled, lavender to pink flowers, each marked with a distinctive yellow-gold eye that gives the plant its common name, blooming alongside bluebonnets in Hill Country wildflower displays. Plants complete their life cycle and set seed by early summer as temperatures rise, then die back and reseed themselves in soil that is not disturbed or heavily mulched. Once established in a compatible thin, rocky, well-drained site, it self-sows reliably year after year and needs no irrigation beyond natural rainfall.

planting.note: Plant rooted offsets or container-grown rosettes in spring into well-drained, dry, alkaline, rocky or clay-loam soil in full sun to light shade; paleleaf yucca is a stemless, slow-growing Texas prairie and woodland-edge endemic best propagated by division.

directions: Plant divisions or container-grown rosettes in well-drained, lean, alkaline soil in full sun to light shade; paleleaf yucca forms a stemless, symmetrical rosette of broad, pale blue-green leaves distinctly softer and paler than most yuccas, with smooth or minimally fibrous leaf margins. A tall flower spike of creamy white, bell-shaped blooms rises 3 to 5 feet above the foliage in late spring, pollinated by the same specialized yucca moths as other Yucca species, and is a striking accent even when the plant is not in bloom. Native to the North Central Texas Blackland Prairie and Cross Timbers, it tolerates heavy clay and limestone soils better than many desert yuccas, as long as drainage is adequate and standing water is avoided. Extremely low maintenance once established, it needs no fertilizer or supplemental water beyond an occasional deep soak in extended drought.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs or rooted softwood cuttings in early spring or fall into average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Thunberg spirea roots readily from cuttings and establishes quickly.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained garden soil in full sun to light shade; Thunberg spirea is among the earliest-blooming of all spireas, opening masses of tiny, five-petaled white flowers along slender, arching branches in very early spring, often before or alongside forsythia, giving rise to its baby's-breath-like common name. Fine-textured, narrow blue-green leaves follow the bloom and often color soft yellow-orange in fall before dropping. The fountain-like, twiggy habit is best left unsheared and only lightly thinned right after flowering, removing a portion of the oldest canes at the base every few years to keep the shrub airy and floriferous rather than dense and shaded out. It tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil once established and is a reliable, low-fuss flowering shrub for foundation plantings, informal hedges, and mixed borders.
